title: Ticket booking
summary: Seat holds, contention and never selling a seat twice.
prompt: Design ticket booking for concerts. Users browse events, hold specific seats for a few minutes while paying, and must never be sold the same seat as someone else.

requirements: Functional: list events and seat maps, hold seats for a few minutes, pay, issue tickets, and release expired holds.
Correctness: never sell a seat twice. The browse view may briefly lag; a seat shown as free can fail to hold.
Non-functional: survive on-sale spikes in which many users want the same few thousand seats at once.
estimation: A big on-sale might see 1M users arrive for 50,000 seats within minutes; the hard part is contention, not volume.
Seat-map reads can reach tens of thousands per second; writes (holds) are bounded by seats × attempts.
Data is small: 10,000 events × 50,000 seats × ~100 bytes ≈ 50 GB.
api: GET /events/{id}/seats → availability, cacheable for a second or two.
POST /holds {eventId, seatIds} → 201 {holdId, expiresAt}, or 409 listing the seats already taken.
POST /orders {holdId, paymentToken} with an Idempotency-Key → confirmed or payment failed; DELETE /holds/{id} releases.
data: seats(event_id, seat_id, status free|held|sold, hold_id, hold_expires_at), primary key (event_id, seat_id).
holds(id, user_id, event_id, expires_at) and orders(id, hold_id UNIQUE, user_id, amount, status).
A relational database, because transactions and conditional row updates are the core requirement.
design: Browse: seat maps from a cache refreshed every second or two; the database stays the source of truth.
Hold: one transaction conditionally updates each requested seat where status is free or its hold has expired. If any seat fails, roll back and return 409.
Pay: charge with an idempotency key, then mark the seats sold where hold_id matches and the hold is still valid.
A virtual waiting room admits users at a controlled rate during on-sales.
deepDives: No double sale: a conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'free' is atomic per row. Lock seats in a consistent order (sorted seat IDs) to avoid deadlocks when holding several.
Expiry: the same conditional update treats an expired hold as free, so correctness never depends on a background job; a sweeper only tidies up.
Payment after expiry: if a payment succeeds after the seat was released and resold, refund automatically, or extend the hold while a payment is in flight.
bottlenecks: Hot rows: shard by event_id so one event’s seats live together and a hold is a single-shard transaction.
Thundering herd at on-sale: waiting room, rate limits, and short-lived cached seat maps.
Bots: per-account limits, challenges at the waiting room, and purchase caps.
tradeoffs: Strong consistency for seat state, eventual for the browse map; users may see a seat that has just gone.
Short holds are fairer but cause more payment-after-expiry cases.
A waiting room adds delay for everyone but protects the database and fairness.

rubric.text: Guaranteed no double-selling with an atomic conditional update or lock.
Modelled holds with expiry that does not depend on a background job for correctness.
Made payment idempotent and handled payment after expiry.
Separated cached browse reads from transactional writes.
Planned for on-sale contention: waiting room and rate limits.
Chose a data store with the transactions needed and said why.
Addressed deadlocks, sharding by event and hot-row contention.
